title: Direct Routing
subtitle: How PSTN2 connects providers peer to peer: lower cost, lower latency, better quality and encryption by default.
endNote: Next: how PSTN2 gives emergency services a caller’s location in real time.

segments.text: Today, a call between two providers often crosses several transit networks on the way.
Every hop adds cost, adds delay, and adds another point of failure.
Transit providers charge for carrying the traffic. So calls end up slower, and more expensive, than they need to be.
PSTN2 lets providers connect directly, cutting out the middlemen.
When an Alpha Telecom customer calls a Bravo Networks customer, the two providers set up a direct media connection.
No transit providers. No extra hops. Just source to destination.
So how does Alpha find Bravo? With PSTN2 number discovery. The customer has dialled 0113 496 0456.
Alpha checks its cache. There is no entry, so it looks the number up in its own copy of Ofcom’s S1 to S9 numbering lists.
The list names Charlie Comms as the Range Holder, with its PSTN2 address. Charlie replies: this number has been ported to Bravo.
Alpha follows the redirect, and Bravo answers: held. Alpha caches the answer, so next time it goes straight to Bravo.
Now Alpha sends Bravo a routing request. Bravo replies with the address and port for a direct SIP invite.
Direct routing removes transit fees.
That could cut per-minute costs by as much as seventy-five percent.
For high-volume carriers, that means millions saved every year. For consumers, it means lower prices.
And the savings begin with the very first direct call.
Removing transit hops cuts latency by seventy-five percent or more.
A traditional call might cross five to seven hops. A direct call uses one.
Lower latency means better call quality, especially for live conversation and video calls.
During call setup, the two providers exchange identity keys, inside the signed routing request and response.
Then a DTLS handshake between the media endpoints creates fresh SRTP keys, unique to this call.
The identity keys prove that each side of the handshake is genuine. The media keys themselves never cross the network.
From then on, all voice and video is encrypted end to end between the providers.
With direct routing and encryption, media never crosses an untrusted network unprotected.
There is no transit provider in the path, so nobody in the middle can listen in.
Lawful interception remains possible, but only with the providers’ cooperation, under proper legal authority.
Customers get privacy by default, not as an optional extra.
Direct connections give providers better control over call quality.
They negotiate codecs, bandwidth and quality directly, in the routing request.
No transit network imposes the lowest common denominator, so HD voice and video can become standard.
As more providers adopt PSTN2, the benefits multiply.
Ten providers can use ninety direct routes, counting each direction between every pair.
A hundred providers can use nearly ten thousand.
Every new participant makes the whole network more valuable.
If a provider does not support PSTN2, the call falls back to traditional routing, automatically.
There is no failure mode, and callers notice nothing.
But when both sides support PSTN2, they get every benefit: lower cost, lower latency, better quality and end-to-end encryption.
Providers can agree formal peering for direct routing, much like peering on the internet.
An agreement can set the technical details, service levels, and any settlement rates.
But unlike traditional telecom interconnects, PSTN2 makes peering easy to set up, and automated to run.
Direct routing also allows geographic optimisation.
If Alpha and Bravo both have equipment in London, their London calls can be connected in London, even if their headquarters are elsewhere.
That cuts long-distance and international transit costs, and improves call quality.
